takeaway: A fall in pCO2 shifts the oxygen-haemoglobin curve to the left: haemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly.

question.text: Which displaces the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve to the left?
question.say: Which of these displaces the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve to the left?

answer.say: The answer is a fall in p C O two.

lines.text: A left shift means haemoglobin holds oxygen tight.
lines.say: A left shift means haemoglobin grips its oxygen tightly, like this strong hero hugging every ball.

lines.text: The CO2 balloon goes flat: a fall in pCO2.
lines.say: The carbon dioxide balloon deflates. A fall in p C O two shifts the curve left.

lines.text: A rise in pH flies the same flag.
lines.say: (laugh) His friend waves the flag for a rise in p H, another left shift.

lines.text: So do cold, less 2,3-DPG, fetal haemoglobin and carbon monoxide.
lines.say: So do a fall in temperature, less two three D P G, fetal haemoglobin, and carbon monoxide.

lines.text: Acidosis, heat, a rise in pCO2 and exercise push it right.
lines.say: Acidosis, heat, a rise in p C O two, and exercise push it right.

lines.text: Remember: a fall in pCO2 shifts the curve to the left.
lines.say: Remember: a fall in p C O two shifts the curve to the left.
